title: Accounts-Receivable Chaser

chase_invoice.description: Given an overdue invoice and the client's history, draft the right next dunning step and (on approval) send it.
chase_invoice._comment_promises: A run of this type is not finished when it has written a good chase — it is finished when a human has been asked to send one. Observed in production 2026-08-10: a chase_invoice run completed, reported success, and told the founder the draft would be waiting in Approvals. Zero approvals were created (the approvals table held zero rows account-wide), nothing was sent, and the $4,800 invoice it had already stamped as chased dropped off the ranked list. `promises` is the kernel-side check, made against the run's own event log rather than against its summary — a summary is a claim, an approval.requested event is evidence. `hold` and `channel: none` are the two ways this ladder legitimately decides to say nothing; every other outcome must show an approval or the run is failed. See promises.ts.

_comment_approvals: `send` used to be declared here at high risk, and it matched every chase this wedge writes — so a first polite reminder on a 180-dollar invoice was declared exactly as serious as a refund, and the founder's queue was a wall of identical red pills. That is what teaches someone to clear a queue without reading it. The blanket entry is gone. An ordinary reminder is now scored from what is actually in it (see risk.ts) and it is still gated, because `send` is one of the harness's own default gate patterns and always has been — nothing here changes WHETHER a human sees it, only how loudly it asks. What stays declared is what the heuristics cannot know from a payload: a final notice is a change of TONE, not of amount, and it is the last email before this stops being a relationship.

workflows.description: The dunning step the policy dictates, given the facts. ALWAYS use this to choose the step; then write the message yourself.
